newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Mediaset eyes satellite theme channels.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Mediaset eyes satellite theme channels.

text.p: Mediaset, the Italian commercial television group controlled by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, said on Wednesday it would like to get into new media technology and had rented space on a new satellite.

But the group, which could be compelled to move one of its three terrestrial channels to satellite in late 1997 under a new media bill that is now before parliament, said it had no immediate plans as current legislation bars it from expanding.
"We could launch new thematic channels from next year," said Soune Wade, Mediaset's director of international affairs.
"We have the know-how...We have already rented a transponder on Hot Bird," she told an industry conference. But she added:
"We can't go ahead because the law is the law...We cannot create. We are at the maximum."
Renting a transponder on the Hot Bird 2 satellite, which becomes operational in early December, costs 7.5 billion lire ($5 million) a year for a 12-year contract.
One transponder could offer six to eight channels.

The new satellite will enable broadcasters to offer dozens of new channels via sophisticated digital technology. Analysts believe the Italian satellite market, a relative infant compared with other European countries, is ripe for growth.

Under the draft legislation, which Mediaset has hotly contested, the group would be required to transfer one of its three terrestrial stations to satellite because of provisions setting a ceiling of 30 percent in any one TV market.
The government estimates that Mediaset has 36 percent of the terrestrial television market.
Wade said that transferring an advertising-supported free station to satellite would not be economically viable.
Mediaset would run into problems with programme rights -- it only has terrestrial rights for its movies -- and would face stiff competition from Italian pay-TV specialist, Telepiu.
"I don't know...whether we could keep it (the channel)," Wade said. "It would be a condemned channel."
Media analysts said investors were undeterred by the regulatory uncertainty. The relatively underdeveloped nature of the market made Italy an attractive opportunity, they said.
"I would expect that we will see, over time, the evolution of a communications society in Italy and probably on a very fast track," said consultant Paul Kagan, the conference organiser.
Analysts judge cable technology too expensive to take off in Italy as it has done in the United States or Britain, but reckon satellite has good prospects and investors will take the risk.
"Italians watch a lot of television and they don't spend a lot of money on pay-TV," said Brian Sturgess, global media strategist at ING Barings in London.
He said the Italian market looked somewhat like Britain's before Rupert Murdoch launched his BSkyB satellite group. BSkyB had huge start-up costs but has grown rapidly.
Eutelsat, which owns the two Hot Birds and plans to launch three more by 1998, giving scope for hundreds of channels, said Italy even lagged behind Iceland with some 700,000 satellite homes.
"Obviously some aspects of the Italian market are worrisome," said one executive from a niche channel looking to expand from northern Europe into Italy. But he added:
"We want a lot of homes. We're talking to everybody." ($1=1513 Lire)
